title: Control plane anatomy
summary: kube-apiserver, etcd, controller-manager and scheduler: what each one owns and what happens without it.

concepts.title: kube-apiserver
concepts.brief:
The API server is the **only** component that talks to etcd. Everything else — kubelet, scheduler, controllers, your `kubectl`, Rancher — goes through its REST API.

That design has consequences you feel in production:

- It is **stateless**, so you can run three of them behind a load balancer and scale horizontally.
- It is the choke point for authentication, authorisation and admission. There is no back door to etcd.
- If it goes down, you lose *control* of the cluster, not the cluster. Running pods keep running; kubelets keep restarting crashed containers from their local view.

It also serves the **watch** API: clients open a long-lived connection and get a stream of add/update/delete events instead of polling. Every controller in the system is built on this.

examples.label: Ask the API server about itself
examples.code:
$ kubectl get --raw /healthz
ok

$ kubectl get --raw '/readyz?verbose' | head -5
[+]ping ok
[+]log ok
[+]etcd ok
[+]informer-sync ok
[+]poststarthook/start-apiserver-admission-initializer ok
examples.note: `/healthz` is liveness, `/readyz` is 'ready to serve traffic'. `readyz` includes an etcd check — a very quick way to tell whether the API server or its datastore is the problem.

examples.label: Watching, the thing every controller does
examples.code:
# a raw watch stream - this is what an informer opens under the hood
$ kubectl get pods -w

# same thing, unwrapped
$ kubectl get --raw '/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods?watch=true&resourceVersion=0'
examples.note: The `resourceVersion` in the response is etcd's revision. A watch resumes from a revision, which is why controllers can restart without replaying the world.

examples.label: In RKE2 it is a static pod
examples.code:
$ ls /var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/pod-manifests/
etcd.yaml  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml

$ crictl ps --name kube-apiserver
CONTAINER      IMAGE          STATE     NAME             POD
8b1f2c0a9d3e   hardened-...   Running   kube-apiserver   kube-apiserver-node1
examples.note: No Deployment, no scheduler involvement — the kubelet reads these files off disk and starts the containers itself.

items.prompt: Which components write directly to etcd in a standard cluster?
choices: Only kube-apiserver
kube-apiserver and kube-controller-manager
kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler and kubelet
Any component holding a valid client certificate
items.explain: Only kube-apiserver. Every other component — including the scheduler and controller-manager — reaches etcd *through* the API server. That is what makes authn/authz/admission unavoidable and lets you audit every change in one place.

items.prompt: The API server is down on all three control-plane nodes. Which of these still work?
choices: Containers that are already running keep running
A kubelet restarts a container that crashed
A Deployment scales up after an HPA decision
A failed node's pods get rescheduled elsewhere
Service traffic keeps flowing through existing kube-proxy rules
items.explain: The data plane is decoupled from the control plane. Kubelets keep their local pod spec and restart containers; kube-proxy's iptables/IPVS rules stay in the kernel. What you lose is *change*: no scheduling, no scaling, no rescheduling, no new Services propagating.

items.prompt: Why can you run three kube-apiservers active/active behind a load balancer, but only one active kube-controller-manager?
choices: The API server is stateless; the controller-manager runs reconcile loops that must not be duplicated, so it uses leader election
The controller-manager holds an exclusive etcd lock at startup
The API server is licensed for HA and the controller-manager is not
kube-proxy can only route to one controller-manager
items.explain: All three API servers can serve reads and writes because state lives in etcd, not in the process. Controller-managers and schedulers all run, but only the leader acts — they hold a Lease in `kube-system` and renew it. Two active controller-managers would fight over the same objects.

items.prompt: Which resource type do the controller-manager and scheduler use in `kube-system` to elect a leader? (the modern one, not the old endpoint/configmap trick)
items.explain: `Lease` objects in `coordination.k8s.io`. `kubectl -n kube-system get lease` shows `kube-controller-manager`, `kube-scheduler`, and one Lease per node for node heartbeats. Older clusters used annotations on an Endpoints or ConfigMap object.

items.prompt: `kubectl get --raw '/readyz?verbose'` shows `[-]etcd failed: reason withheld` but `/healthz` returns ok. What does that tell you?
choices: The API server process is alive but cannot reach its datastore, so it will not serve traffic
etcd is healthy and the API server is deadlocked
The certificate for etcd expired an hour ago, specifically
Nothing — readyz is always noisy on RKE2
items.explain: Liveness (`healthz`) and readiness (`readyz`) are deliberately different: the process is running, but a dependency check failed, so the load balancer should stop sending it traffic. Next step is to look at etcd directly rather than restarting the API server.

concepts.title: etcd and quorum
concepts.brief:
etcd is a distributed key-value store using the **Raft** consensus algorithm. Every write goes to the leader and must be acknowledged by a **majority** of members before it is committed.

Majority is why member counts are odd:

- 3 members tolerate 1 failure (quorum 2)
- 5 members tolerate 2 failures (quorum 3)
- 4 members also tolerate only 1 failure — an extra member with no extra safety, and more write latency

Lose quorum and etcd goes **read-only-ish**: writes fail, so the whole cluster freezes for changes. This is the single most important failure mode to understand on a self-managed cluster.

etcd is also latency-sensitive: it fsyncs to disk on every commit. Slow disks show up as `apply request took too long` warnings and then as a laggy, flaky API server.

examples.label: Health of the members (RKE2 paths)
examples.code:
$ export ETCDCTL_API=3
$ export ETCDCTL_ENDPOINTS=https://127.0.0.1:2379
$ export ETCDCTL_CACERT=/var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/tls/etcd/server-ca.crt
$ export ETCDCTL_CERT=/var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/tls/etcd/server-client.crt
$ export ETCDCTL_KEY=/var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/tls/etcd/server-client.key

$ etcdctl endpoint status --cluster -w table
+---------------------------+------------------+---------+---------+-----------+
|         ENDPOINT          |        ID        | VERSION | DB SIZE | IS LEADER |
+---------------------------+------------------+---------+---------+-----------+
| https://10.0.0.11:2379    | 8e9e05c52164694d |  3.5.13 |  412 MB |     true  |
| https://10.0.0.12:2379    | 91bc3c398fb3c146 |  3.5.13 |  412 MB |    false  |
| https://10.0.0.13:2379    | fd422379fda50e48 |  3.5.13 |  411 MB |    false  |
+---------------------------+------------------+---------+---------+-----------+

examples.label: The warning that precedes an outage
examples.code:
etcd  W | etcdserver: read-only range request "key:\"/registry/pods/\" " took too long (2.1s) to execute
etcd  W | etcdserver: apply request took too long (1.8s) [expected 100ms]
apiserver E | Timeout: Too large resource version / etcdserver: request timed out
examples.note: Almost always disk latency or a database that needs defragmenting — not CPU. Put etcd on its own fast disk.

examples.label: Snapshots are your restore path
examples.code:
# RKE2 takes these automatically; on-demand:
$ rke2 etcd-snapshot save --name pre-upgrade

$ rke2 etcd-snapshot list
NAME                    LOCATION                                              SIZE      CREATED
pre-upgrade-node1-...   /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/db/snapshots/...          412M      2026-05-02T09:14:03Z
examples.note: Restoring an etcd snapshot rolls the *entire cluster state* back to that moment. It is a cluster-wide time machine, not a per-namespace undo.

items.prompt: You run a 5-member etcd cluster. Two nodes are down for maintenance and a third dies. What happens?
choices: Quorum is lost (3 of 5 needed); writes fail and the cluster stops accepting changes
The remaining two members elect a leader and continue normally
etcd automatically shrinks the member list to 2 and keeps quorum
Reads fail but writes continue from the local cache
items.explain: Quorum for 5 members is 3. With only 2 alive there is no majority, so no leader can be elected and no write can commit. Existing workloads keep running, but the cluster is frozen until you restore a member or recover from a snapshot.

items.prompt: Why is a 4-member etcd cluster a worse choice than a 3-member one?
choices: Both tolerate only 1 failure, but 4 members add write latency and a larger split-brain surface
4 members cannot elect a leader at all
Raft requires a prime number of members
4 members tolerate 2 failures but lose read consistency
items.explain: Quorum of 4 is 3, so you can still only lose one member — identical fault tolerance to a 3-node cluster, but every write must be acknowledged by more peers. Even numbers buy you nothing.

items.prompt: Put a successful etcd write in order.
steps: kube-apiserver sends the write to the etcd leader
The leader appends the entry to its Raft log and replicates it to followers
A majority of members persist the entry and acknowledge
The leader commits the entry and bumps the global revision
kube-apiserver returns success with the new resourceVersion
items.explain: The commit happens only after a majority acknowledges — that is the whole safety guarantee. The revision that comes back becomes the object's `resourceVersion`, which is how watches resume and how optimistic concurrency works.

items.prompt: Logs show `apply request took too long (1.8s) [expected 100ms]` on all three etcd members, and the API server is intermittently timing out. Most likely cause?
choices: Disk write latency (fsync) on the etcd volume
A CNI misconfiguration dropping packets between nodes
kube-scheduler thrashing over unschedulable pods
Too many namespaces in the cluster
items.explain: etcd fsyncs every committed entry. When all members degrade together it is nearly always storage — shared/spinning disks, noisy neighbours, or a database that has grown and needs defrag/compaction. Check `etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds` and give etcd a dedicated SSD.

items.prompt: Someone deleted a production namespace. You have an etcd snapshot from 20 minutes ago. What is the honest consequence of restoring it?
choices: The entire cluster state rolls back 20 minutes — every object created or changed since then is lost
Only the deleted namespace is restored, other changes are preserved
Restoring merges the snapshot with current state, newest wins
Nothing changes until you restart the kubelets
items.explain: An etcd snapshot is the whole keyspace. Restore is all-or-nothing and cluster-wide. That is why per-object backups (Velero, GitOps manifests in Git) matter — etcd snapshots are for cluster disasters, not for undoing a `kubectl delete`.

concepts.title: kube-controller-manager
concepts.brief:
One binary running dozens of independent control loops in goroutines. Each loop watches some objects and works to make the world match the spec.

Controllers you meet in incidents:

- **node controller** — marks nodes `NotReady` when heartbeats stop, then evicts their pods after a toleration timeout
- **replicaset / deployment controllers** — create and delete pods to hit the replica count
- **endpointslice controller** — keeps Service backends in sync with ready pod IPs
- **namespace controller** — deletes everything in a terminating namespace
- **garbage collector** — deletes objects whose owner disappeared
- **service account / token, PV binder, job, cronjob, ttl-after-finished...**

All of them share the same shape: *watch → compare desired vs actual → act → repeat*. None of them assume they only run once, which is why the system heals after restarts.

examples.label: Node goes quiet, controller reacts
examples.code:
# node stops sending Lease heartbeats
$ kubectl get nodes
NAME    STATUS     ROLES    AGE   VERSION
node3   NotReady   <none>   80d   v1.31.4+rke2r1

# after 5m (default toleration), pods are marked for eviction
$ kubectl get pod -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=node3
NAME        READY   STATUS        NODE
api-7c9d    1/1     Terminating   node3
examples.note: `--node-monitor-grace-period` (40s) decides *NotReady*; the `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute` toleration with `tolerationSeconds: 300` decides when pods actually go.

examples.label: Which controllers are enabled
examples.code:
$ kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-controller-manager-node1 -o yaml | grep -A3 'controllers'
    - --controllers=*,bootstrapsigner,tokencleaner
    - --leader-elect=true
    - --node-monitor-grace-period=40s

items.prompt: What is the shared shape of every Kubernetes controller?
choices: Watch objects, compare desired spec to observed status, act to close the gap, repeat forever
Receive an RPC from the scheduler, execute it once, report back
Poll etcd every 30 seconds and apply a diff
Subscribe to a message queue and process events exactly once
items.explain: This is *level-triggered reconciliation*. Controllers act on observed state, not on a stream of commands they must not miss. Missing an event is survivable — the next resync sees the same gap and fixes it. It is why the system converges instead of drifting.

items.prompt: Match the controller to what it does.
pairs: Marks nodes NotReady and evicts their pods
Keeps Service backends in sync with ready pod IPs
Deletes objects whose owner no longer exists
Empties a namespace stuck in Terminating
items.explain: Knowing which loop owns a symptom cuts debugging time in half: a Service with no endpoints is an endpointslice-controller/readiness question, while a namespace stuck Terminating is almost always a finalizer the namespace controller is waiting on.

items.prompt: A node loses network connectivity. With defaults, roughly how long until its pods are marked for deletion so they can run elsewhere?
choices: ~40 seconds to NotReady, then ~5 minutes before eviction
Immediately — the scheduler reschedules on the next loop
~10 seconds total
Never, unless you drain the node manually
items.explain: `--node-monitor-grace-period=40s` flips the node to NotReady; the taint `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute` is then tolerated for 300s by default before pods are evicted. Total: roughly 5m40s. Shorten `tolerationSeconds` per-pod if your app needs faster failover — but expect more churn on flaky networks.

items.prompt: A node running a StatefulSet pod becomes unreachable. Why does the replacement pod stay `Pending` instead of starting elsewhere?
choices: StatefulSet identity must be unique, and the control plane cannot prove the old pod is really gone while the node is unreachable
StatefulSets are not managed by the controller-manager
The scheduler refuses to place pods with PVCs
The default toleration for StatefulSets is infinite
items.explain: Unreachable is not the same as dead. Starting `web-0` twice could corrupt shared storage, so Kubernetes waits: the pod stays Terminating until the node returns or you force-delete it (or the node object is removed). This surprises people every time a node partitions.

concepts.title: kube-scheduler in one loop
concepts.brief:
The scheduler watches for pods with an empty `spec.nodeName` and decides where they go. It does **not** start containers — it writes a **Binding**, and the kubelet on that node takes it from there.

Each pod goes through two phases:

- **Filter** (predicates): which nodes *could* run this pod? Resources, taints, node selectors, affinity, volume topology.
- **Score** (priorities): of those, which is *best*? Spread across zones, least-requested resources, image already present.

It scores on **requests**, never on actual usage. A node at 95% real CPU with only small requests booked looks empty to the scheduler.

examples.label: The decision, visible in events
examples.code:
$ kubectl describe pod api-7c9d | tail -6
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
  ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  62s   default-scheduler  0/6 nodes are available:
           2 Insufficient cpu, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint {node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: },
           1 node(s) didn't match pod anti-affinity rules.
examples.note: Read this message as the filter phase reporting why each node was rejected. It is the single most useful line in scheduling debugging.

examples.label: Bypassing the scheduler entirely
examples.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pinned
spec:
  nodeName: node3        # set directly - scheduler never sees this pod
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
examples.note: Setting `nodeName` skips scheduling, and skips every filter with it: no resource check, no taint check. The kubelet on node3 just runs it — or the pod stays Pending forever if that node does not exist.

items.prompt: The scheduler picks node2 for a pod. What does it actually do next?
choices: Writes a Binding object to the API server, setting the pod's nodeName; the kubelet on node2 then starts it
Connects to node2's kubelet over gRPC and asks it to start the pod
Tells containerd on node2 to pull the image
Updates etcd directly with the pod placement
items.explain: Everything is mediated by the API server. The scheduler's whole job is to fill in one field. The kubelet on node2 is watching for pods bound to itself and picks it up — no component ever pushes work to a node.

items.prompt: node1 sits at 92% actual CPU but its pods only *request* 300m total. A new pod requests 2 CPU. What does the scheduler think?
choices: node1 has plenty of allocatable CPU left and is a fine candidate
node1 is full and will be filtered out
It checks live metrics from the metrics-server and skips node1
It refuses to schedule until utilisation drops
items.explain: Scheduling is a bookkeeping exercise over **requests**, not a load balancer over real usage. This is exactly how you end up with hot nodes: requests set far below real consumption. Fixing it means setting honest requests (or using a descheduler / VPA), not tuning the scheduler.

items.prompt: The scheduler first eliminates impossible nodes, then ranks the survivors. Name the *first* phase.
items.explain: Filter (historically 'predicates') narrows candidates to feasible nodes; Score (historically 'priorities') ranks them. `FailedScheduling` messages are the filter phase explaining itself.

items.prompt: You set `spec.nodeName` directly on a pod. What do you give up?
choices: Resource fit checking — it can be admitted onto a full node
Taint and toleration enforcement by the scheduler
The ability for the kubelet to run it at all
Rescheduling if that node is drained or dies
items.explain: The kubelet still runs it (option 3 is wrong), but you have opted out of every scheduling guarantee. The kubelet may still reject it later if the node genuinely lacks resources — you get an `OutOfcpu` pod instead of a clean Pending. Static pods and some DaemonSet-like tooling use this deliberately.
